    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Enterprise AI spending is growing faster than the number of organizations paying for it, according to a newly introduced Menlo Ventures report that points to a shift from buying access for employees to financing work performed by agents.
    • The venture capital firm's 2026 State of Enterprise AI report estimates deployment spending reached a $176.8 billion annualized run rate by September, up from $33 billion in 2025.
    • A larger bill can reflect broader use inside an organization, but it does not independently establish that the additional work is useful or profitable.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Enterprise AI spending is growing faster than the number of organizations paying for it, according to a newly introduced Menlo Ventures report that points to a shift from buying access for employees to financing work performed by agents.

    The venture capital firm's 2026 State of Enterprise AI report estimates deployment spending reached a $176.8 billion annualized run rate by September, up from $33 billion in 2025. The share of enterprises paying for AI rose from 55% to 65%.

    A larger bill can reflect broader use inside an organization, but it does not independently establish that the additional work is useful or profitable.

    Menlo's methodology describes revenue figures as annualized run rates. The $176.8 billion estimate therefore should not be read as $176.8 billion already spent during the first nine months of 2026.

    In a recent development, the report also distinguishes unusually heavy spenders from the typical respondent. Average reported spending reached 4.7 times the prior year's level, while the median reached 2.2 times. That gap suggests a smaller group of large spenders drove the average substantially.

    In a recent development, the practical implication is that an industry growth figure may be a poor benchmark for an individual organization's budget. Buyers need to understand their own workload growth and the results it produces.

    "Agents are changing the economics of software," Menlo principal Derek Xiao remarked in the firm's announcement.

    Menlo reports that agents account for 80% of tokens on OpenRouter, a service providing access to multiple models. That measures activity on one platform, rather than all enterprise AI use. Token consumption also measures processing volume, rather than completed business outcomes.

    Recent findings suggest that an agent that makes repeated attempts can consume more resources without delivering proportionately more value. For procurement teams, the relevant comparison is consequently the cost of completing acceptable work, including the review it requires.

    According to recent reports, menlo estimates that Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google capture 69% of enterprise AI deployment spending. That measure is distinct from their shares of enterprise language-model API spending, a narrower category. The figures should not be used interchangeably.

    The report draws on a Morning Consult survey of nearly 400 U.S. enterprise decision-makers responsible for more than $4 billion in AI spending. Market totals are modeled estimates informed by surveys, public filings, and third-party reports. Menlo discloses investments in Anthropic and OpenRouter.

    In a recent development, A separate announcement from Information Services Group describes buyers putting more emphasis on the economics and reliability of production deployments. ISG notes ongoing security and observability work remains necessary as organizations scale.

    In a recent development, that provides a useful distinction between market demand and business value. Suppliers can generate growing revenue while customers still determine which deployments justify the cost.

    Recent findings suggest that for enterprise leaders, the latest spending estimate strengthens the case for examining usage beyond license counts. It leaves the harder purchasing question with the customer: How much worthwhile work did the increased spending actually buy?

    Breaking: Phishing Threats Totaled 7.3 Billion in Q3 2026

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (500 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • E-mail phishing threats reached 7.3 billion in Q3 2026, with September activity increasing 41% from August, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence.
    • According to a report from Microsoft Threat Intelligence and the Microsoft Defender Security Research Team, phishing detections reached nearly 3 billion in September alone.
    • The findings also highlighted changes in attacker techniques, including business-service impersonation, credential theft, and social engineering through Microsoft Teams.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    E-mail phishing threats reached 7.3 billion in Q3 2026, with September activity increasing 41% from August, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence.

    According to a report from Microsoft Threat Intelligence and the Microsoft Defender Security Research Team, phishing detections reached nearly 3 billion in September alone.

    The findings also highlighted changes in attacker techniques, including business-service impersonation, credential theft, and social engineering through Microsoft Teams.

    The Redmond-based firm recognized approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of tracked business services during Q3.

    It has been revealed that docuSign was the most frequently spoofed brand in September, accounting for 29% of the month's tracked spoofing activity. Adobe, SurveyMonkey, and Barracuda also experienced increases toward the end of the quarter.

    The research found that some malicious messages were delivered despite failing e-mail authentication checks and being identified as threats.

    In September, tenant- or user-level security overrides applied to 63% of these messages with a recorded security outcome — most involved tenant-level exceptions.

    Microsoft warned that overly broad exceptions intended to support legitimate business communications can weaken protection against impersonation attacks.

    The organization emphasized that these findings do not establish whether recipients opened the messages or whether accounts were compromised.

    Microsoft also recorded approximately 141,000 malicious Teams call attempts during Q3.

    Attackers increasingly used ordinary personal names instead of explicitly impersonating IT support personnel. Such display names accounted for 46% of an observed sample in July, rising to 88% in September.

    Meanwhile, QR code phishing declined 67% compared to Q2, totaling roughly 12.1 million attacks.

    CAPTCHA-gated phishing activity increased toward the end of the quarter, reaching 3.1 million detected attacks in September. SVG attachments played a significant role in the increase.

    Credential theft remained the primary objective of malicious attachment campaigns, with approximately 94% to 96% of payload-based attacks directing owners to phishing sites or fraudulent sign-in pages.

    Microsoft recommended reviewing Exchange Online Protection and Defender for Office 365 configurations, enabling Safe Links and Safe Attachments, and strengthening authentication protections.

    The organization also advised organizations to review security exceptions and verify the identities of external Teams contacts before responding to suspicious requests.

    For more information, go to the Microsoft blog post.

    #180822. Alexis Nikole Nelson, aka the Black Forager, Makes Nature Her Buffet

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1992 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Saveur ↗ Open Full Page

    Alexis Nikole Nelson, aka the Black Forager, Makes Nature Her Buffet

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1992 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that this is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people.
    • In a recent development, alexis Nicole Nelson’s life mantra is simple: “Don’t put things in your face hole unless you know what they are!” This mostly applies to foraging wild foods, something she has been doing since she was a kid with her mom and has since turned into a flourishing career and community.
    • In a recent development, nelson’s journey to becoming the Black Forager started with an interest in vegetarianism as a 5-year-old, which, at the time, was discouraged by her family.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that this is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people. This interview series will dive deep into their food routines, including dinner party strategies, cherished cookbooks, and the memorable bites they’d hop on a flight for.

    In a recent development, alexis Nicole Nelson’s life mantra is simple: “Don’t put things in your face hole unless you know what they are!” This mostly applies to foraging wild foods, something she has been doing since she was a kid with her mom and has since turned into a flourishing career and community. She has showcased her adventures and recipes as @blackforager since 2018 (with millions of curious followers across Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube) and now in her debut cookbook, Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! This comprehensive guide to finding and cooking with ingredients from your backyard or nearby forests and fields is organized by season and anchored by Nelson’s vibrant personality and boundless energy, encouraging readers to get out of their comfort zones and educate themselves on edible plants hiding in plain sight.

    In a recent development, nelson’s journey to becoming the Black Forager started with an interest in vegetarianism as a 5-year-old, which, at the time, was discouraged by her family. “You have to finish growing first!” Nelson recalls her mom saying. Nelson ate meat products to keep from wasting food her parents prepared until she was 12, when she decided to start packing her own lunches. “It was a lot of undressed Boca burgers and French fries. It was a bleak time,” she admits with a laugh. She went fully vegan at 24 and hasn’t looked back.

    I am not a very outdoorsy person, but I was captivated by the whimsical way Nelson goes about foraging and sharing online, and even more so after chatting with her on a recent Zoom call. When I asked for easy gateway foraging ideas, she immediately suggested field garlic or onion grass: “I am a biased party, because that is the first forageable that my mom taught me. Once you notice it, you see it everywhere, and it has a foolproof test, which is the smell test. If you break it and it doesn’t very fragrantly smell of onions and garlic, you have the wrong plant. Easy, easy!” She recommended looking for little purple flowers or round pink spiky balls, and on my next walk with my dogs, I spotted some. I haven’t picked and cooked with any yet, but now I’m on the lookout (and smell-out) for this abundant allium and initiative on pairing it with the maitake bacon recipe from her book. Nelson suggested making a “BLT-adjacent sandwich with whatever mild greens are in season, a slice of tomato, and maitake bacon on toasty sourdough.”.

    It has been revealed that whether you’re a foraging beginner or an expert, Nelson’s edition of Amused Bouche will be equally eye-opening and mouthwatering. Read on for her adventures and misadventures in the fields and in her home kitchen.

    If you could only eat one thing 24/7/365, what would it be?

    I love a tofu scramble and mixing in whatever is in season, and I bring home mushrooms, greens, and aromatics. In the springtime, it’ll be ramp leaves and oyster mushrooms. In the summer, it’s chanterelle and bicolor bolete with some nodding onion flowers from my front yard. As we move into winter, I’m thankful that we get enoki mushrooms pretty consistently all throughout the season in the woods. I do a combo of firm silken and super-firm tofu because I want the best of both worlds. Eggs don’t just have one texture; the whites and yolks are different, and I always want to try to get as close to eggs as I can with my tofu textures. I’m perpetually on a search for a forageable legume that I can make my own tofu with. One of my friends, Jesse Akozbek (@feralforaging), makes tofu with black walnuts.

    What’s the first thing you learned how to cook?

    According to recent reports, the first thing that I remember cooking is baking cakes with my dad—usually just a basic frosted vanilla cake. My mom used to be a cool head-honcho character at Procter & Gamble, and she would be gone for two or three weeks at a time for work. We’d bake the cake the night before [she got back], frost it, and then just before she came home, we’d leave the cake out and hide.

    How about your latest kitchen adventure?

    I broke out my food mill because I went a little overboard harvesting cornelian cherries with my fiancé this year. They’re fun to harvest, and we brought a step stool to reach more and ended up going home with a couple gallons of fruit. It’s all fun and games until you see them all on the counter and realize they’re gonna go bad so I gotta figure out what I’m doing with all of this. I thought of doing a glacé cornelian cherry like I’ve done with chestnuts before, but the water content of the cherries is so high that when I simmered them in a sugar syrup, they just disintegrated and disappeared. I tried to stir it carefully, but it all just turned into goo. I fished them out with my little spider, put them in my food mill, and ground it. They have big ol’ pits on the inside, and I am not trying to eat any of those. It was an applesauce consistency in the end, but like what if applesauce had dreams? What if applesauce was the star of a Studio Ghibli movie? I made cornelian cherry shortcakes with it, and my fiancé was like, “So I’ve had three…” and we realized that when you eat a lot of fruit and fiber at once, you remember it later. I also saved the flavored syrup that was created after straining out all of the goopy fruits, and I am saving it specifically for making Shirley Temples!

    What’s your treat-yourself splurge?

    My favorite way to treat myself is getting dinner with my fiancé at Agni, an amazing Bengali American fusion restaurant here in Columbus, led by my friend, chef Avishar Barua! They have these french fries that take three days to make, and I—no joke—dream about them sometimes.

    What’s your most cherished cookbook?

    Marie Viljoen’s Forage, Harvest, Feast is the cookbook that showed me as a recent college graduate that foraging, the weird thing I’ve been doing since childhood, could become such elevated cuisine. It’s absolutely stunning, and she is a recipe and photography genius—she does it all! I remember checking that book out from the library for the first time and my jaw dropping at how she used foraged foods in ways I had never even let myself consider. She gets shouted out in my cookbook because I used a few of her recipes as a jumping-off point then over time I started changing things to make them my own. A decade later, it becomes something different but still has the heart of that original recipe, like my milkweed nectar is definitely the child of her milkweed cordial! Her book was eye-opening for me even before I knew this was what I was going to end up making my career, back when it was something I just did because I loved it and I was a poor recent grad. A really great way to spruce up a 59-cent pack of ramen is wild greens and mushrooms!

    Is there a cooking disaster that made you swear off a dish forever?

    I keep doing this thing where I start fermenting drinks and then travel, which is dumb. Don’t do that! My most explosive ferment was actually not mine, it was a gift from fellow foraging friend Gabrielle Cerberville (@chaoticforager). She very kindly brought me a bottle of her wild plum wine, and I did not put it straight into the fridge because I was not using my noggin. Three days later, I went to open it to pair with dinner, and it was like my world was in slow motion and it was just a geyser everywhere! Wine on the ceiling, wine on the walls, a lot of wine on the floor, a lot of wine on me. I cleaned it up sadly, shooing my pets away. No drunk pets! I also had a milkweed cordial explode, which meant I had to scrub sticky pink off every single thing in the refrigerator. Do not recommend it.

    Which nostalgic foods from childhood bring you the most comfort?

    Recent findings suggest that I grew up in the Cincinnati area, so there will be a soft spot in my heart for Cincinnati chili forever. It’s just ingrained within me. Thankfully Skyline has vegan rice and beans using the same spices that you can also put onto pasta like a wild Ohioan. That will always taste like a Friday evening with my dad, because my mom is from Upcoming England and famously hates Cincinnati chili. I think calling it a chili was maybe its biggest downfall—when you learn about the history behind it and how it’s actually the child of a Greek meat sauce, suddenly the spice palette makes so much more sense. I think people would be so much cooler with that, but everyone’s expecting Tex-Mex chili, and that is not what you are signing up for!

    When you’re playing dinner party DJ, what’s spinning?

    There was a podcast I was obsessed with called The Dinner Party Download a decade ago, and I named my playlist after that. It has been evolving throughout the past 10 years and has Mitski, which I know feels sad for a dinner party but it’s mellow, some alt-J, Bill Withers, The Contours. A lot of Motown-era music, like The Supremes, Stevie Wonder, The Four Tops, Staple Singers. And then Janelle Monáe, Kate Nash, “Rhapsody in Blue” by George Gershwin is thrown in there. I go all over the place, but I think it creates a general buzzy atmosphere. I don’t want it to necessarily be as dancey as a dance party, but I also don’t want people to fall asleep, either.

    What is your biggest entertaining flex to impress guests?

    I really love plating things and cutting things into fun shapes and making them look pretty. I took a cooking class in Japan with Elizabeth Andoh, a very prolific cookbook writer, a couple of years ago, and after my fiancé and I walked out of it, we were just like, “Dang, our food’s real ugly!” A huge part of her class was how much presentation matters and how the first way that you are consuming the food is with your sight, with your eyes, so why not make it look cute?

    Tell me about a meal so good you would hop on a flight to relive it.

    While my fiancé and I were in Florence for a friend’s wedding, we knew that Italy, historically, was not the easiest place to be vegan. You can find things but maybe not that many things, and maybe not the things that look as good as the things everybody else is eating. So I was big sad the entire time until we stumbled into a tiny hole-in-the-wall vegan restaurant called Il Vegano. We found it on Google by searching “vegan restaurants near me,” and it had the best pasta with tomato sauce and tiramisù that either of us have ever had. Mind you, my fiancé is not vegan and very much could still eat real tiramisù and did on that trip. And the night ended with us essentially begging in broken Italian for the head chef to write a cookbook. We waddled back to our hotel saying it was the best meal we’ve ever had.

    This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

    #180803. The Breakfast at Tiffany’s NYC Townhouse Sells for $11.5 Million

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (367 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elledecor ↗ Open Full Page

    The Breakfast at Tiffany’s NYC Townhouse Sells for $11.5 Million

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (367 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Elledecor

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that holly Golightly might have had questionable taste in men, but she had a keen eye for real estate.
    • In May 2025, the five-story residence hit the market for $15 million, following a total overhaul that included a slew of luxe upgrades, such as a new roof terrace and an elevator.
    • Set on a tree-lined block between Lexington and Third Avenues, the East 73rd Street home is distinguished by its Tiffany Blue front door and matching window casings.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that holly Golightly might have had questionable taste in men, but she had a keen eye for real estate. Memorably portrayed by Audrey Hepburn in Breakfast at Tiffany’s, Golightly lived in a handsome Upper East Side brownstone that had been subdivided into apartments. Though the 1961 classic film shot its interior scenes on a Los Angeles soundstage, the exterior of the New York City townhouse served as a backdrop throughout the movie.

    In May 2025, the five-story residence hit the market for $15 million, following a total overhaul that included a slew of luxe upgrades, such as a new roof terrace and an elevator. Although StreetEasy listed the property as “in contract” last December, its official sale date is November 11, 2026. In the end, the two-family house traded hands for $11.5 million, roughly 23 percent off the original price, per Realtor.com.

    Set on a tree-lined block between Lexington and Third Avenues, the East 73rd Street home is distinguished by its Tiffany Blue front door and matching window casings. Built in 1866 by architect John Sexton, the Italianate-style landmark encompasses nearly 4,500 square feet and has four bedrooms in total, three in the main residence—which spans the top four floors—and one in the garden-level apartment, which has its own separate entrance.

    The seller was retired beverage executive Joseph Harkins, who acquired the property in 2015 for $7.4 million and spearheaded a complete transformation that modernized the interiors while still preserving the house’s 19th-century charm. The project even included excavating the basement level, which now has nearly eight-foot ceilings, a powder room, a second laundry room, and a wine cellar.

    In a recent development, outside, the 470-square-foot rear garden is fully enclosed by Walpole lattice fencing and sports stonework paving. It will no doubt be the scene of plenty of “Breakfasts” for the home’s newest steward.

    It has been revealed that geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest, Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A lot of us commiserate about commuting into the office, but there are a few positives to seeing your coworkers regularly, like finding your fellow movie buffs to discuss the latest films with, or bonding with the colleagues you grab drinks with after work. Another upside? Your group may do white elephant gift exchanges, Secret Santa, or at the very least, have an office holiday party. If you are doing a present swap this season, finding creative, affordable gifts for your coworkers could be tricky.

    First, there’s determining the budget; then it’s figuring out whether to get them something practical, fun, edible, or just plain silly. Our thoughtful recommendation is to get a gift they can use immediately or leave at work, like a cute tissue box cover, hand warmers (because the office is always cold), or even a small diffuser that makes the air around them smell better. We found 35 such items they’ll love, and if they truly want to, they could bring and use them at home too.

    Anthropologie has the most adorable mouse pads for the coworker who loves color and whimsy. This one is perfect for book lovers, but we also love the olive and sardines mouse pads.

    The office’s coffee and tea options are typically average, so make their mornings feel more premium with these fancy tea bags. “I got these at work one year, and I ended up falling in love with the tea brand,” Senior Commerce Editor Marina Liao says. “Not only are the tea bags so cute (I feel bad throwing them out when I’m done), but the steeped tea is also highly aromatic and has depth—much better than the standard bags in the office.”.

    The best gifts for coworkers are the ones they didn’t know they needed until they actually have the item in their hands—and can’t ever part with it. “Rechargeable hand warmers are a sleeper hit when I give them as gifts around the holidays,” states Managing Editor Sarah Esgro. “People always come back and thank me again because they didn’t realize how much they needed them. They’re sleek, can be easily tucked into a pocket, and don’t burn your hands the way that the disposable ones can. I even gave them to a coworker whose hands were chronically cold in the office, and she used them all year long!”.

    Recent findings suggest that make your manager laugh with this cheeky glass cup, complete with a wooden lid and a reusable straw. It's perfect for iced coffees, matcha lattes, and more.

    According to recent reports, every group has a crafty team member, which makes this LEGO set a good gift to give. They can build it at work during their lunch break and display it on their desk. Best of all, they don’t have to worry about their florals or greenery dying when they come back from the holiday break.

    The portable lunch box options for adults aren’t nearly as cute as the ones for kids, so we went on the hunt for a nice one and found this pick from Kate Spade Fresh York. It packs just the right amount of style while still feeling functional, so if your coworker always brings their lunch from home, give them a lunch box they won’t cringe at.

    Professional chefs formulated this genius hand scrub. It neutralizes any lingering odors on your hands after a long day of cooking. “I snagged a bottle for a friend of mine who loves to cook, and kept a bottle for myself," Associate Shopping Editor Janae McKenzie notes. "It’s basically replaced my typical hand soap; it feels so luxurious, and makes my hands smell and feel amazing, no matter how much garlic I chopped that day.”.

    A blanket is a safe gift for anyone, and if your office tends to run super cold, like ours, a little fluffiness in their cubicle will be very welcome. This furry blanket from Madison Park adds some elegance and softness, making them feel a bit more comfortable at their desk.

    In a recent development, for the days when work gets stressful, this easy-to-use Buddha Board is the perfect at-desk escape. With a refillable water brush, they can paint any design they choose on a canvas that evaporates in minutes. No muss, no fuss, just endless creativity to reset their brain.

    According to recent reports, we can't get enough of these cheeky cocktail napkins with the ingredients for a perfect Caesar salad. The coworker who's always shaking up a salad bowl around lunchtime will get a kick out of this.

    Recent findings suggest that the personality hire is a key role in any office dynamic. Say thank you to the person who keeps things fun with this chic game box, complete with playing cards, dice, and a classy velvet lining.

    Putting together the staff holiday party is no easy task. Thank the coworker responsible for this finishing touch for the office Christmas tree: a set of scented tree stems. They complete the festive atmosphere by bringing the scent of fir and spruce to the office.

    Sources indicate that this calming bonsai plant does well in low-light, so it's great for office environments. Brighten up their desk and give them something to look forward to when they come in each morning. You can even name it for an extra personal touch.

    According to recent reports, we all have one coworker who can't go a day without a Diet Coke. Help them bring that energy home with this cute candle that smells just like their favorite drink. It has a cola scent they'll love when they reach for their fizzy pick-me-up.

    If your coworker travels for work a lot, gift them this flight essential that McKenzie swears by. “I never go to bed or travel without this thing anymore," McKenzie says.     In a recent development, though there's no harm in buying pre-ground beans, any coffee-based drink will taste much more flavorful with freshly ground beans.     #180776. Tech Report: What to Watch After Finishing MobLand

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (801 w)
    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: What to Watch After Finishing MobLand

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (801 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • MobLand season 2 has come to an end.
    • The obvious choice, if you haven't seen it already, is the other Guy Ritchie series.
    • Industry observers note that when an aristocratic army officer returns home after unexpectedly inheriting his family's estate instead of his older brother, he promptly discovers that it's at the heart of a notorious drug empire.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    MobLand season 2 has come to an end. (For now, at least—Tom Hardy and his motley crew have already started working on the third season.) Fortunately, there's an excellent selection of reveals on Netflix that'll fill that gory Guy Ritchie–crime thriller–shaped void in your weekend watchlist. Here's our pick of the five best ones that you should stream now that season 2 is over. And if you haven’t yet, make sure to read our breakdown of MobLand’s explosive season 2 finale—and that cliffhanger.

    The obvious choice, if you haven't seen it already, is the other Guy Ritchie series. The Gentlemen similarly revolves around a large mob family, has a lot of gore, and has the very same wicked sense of humor.

    Industry observers note that when an aristocratic army officer returns home after unexpectedly inheriting his family's estate instead of his older brother, he promptly discovers that it's at the heart of a notorious drug empire. While he initially tries to shrug it off, he quickly becomes more involved in the criminal underworld than he imagined he would ... and it seems it comes more naturally to him than he'd have hoped.

    The Gentlemen is twisty, wildly entertaining, and will be the closest you'll get to something that feels like MobLand, even though the indicates are narratively quite different.

    It has been revealed that dept. Q is another Netflix original that packs a punch – adapted from the Department Q novel series, it's a crazy crime thriller that only has one season so far, so is easy to catch up on (though a second is on the way).

    After a top-rated detective returns to work from an attack that left his partner paralyzed and another policeman dead, he finds himself caught up in the investigation into a cold case that completely takes hold of him.

    The plot, the sharp sarcastic writing and the way the whole show looks are enough to make Dept. Q an excellent watch, but it's the cast (led by an outstandingly complex performance from Matthew Goode) that makes this one particularly special.

    The spy thriller with the sharpest sense of humor, the most enthralling fight scenes—and, somehow amidst all the explosions—a whole lot of heart. It can be none other than Black Doves, Netflix's original espionage series that has quickly become one of the streamer's best-loved shows.

    Industry observers note that helen Webb, a spy working for an organization called the Black Doves in an undercover marriage to a politician, has her position compromised, and mostly simple”'spy wife life” upended, when her lover is assassinated. In order to protect her and the secrecy of the Black Doves, her supervisor calls in an old friend to save her and sort out the mystery. However, the web of deceit proves unexpectedly complex and the three are soon in over their heads.

    Other than being excellently acted (thanks to the legendary Keira Knightley, Ben Whishaw, Sarah Lancashire, and the supporting cast) and delightfully explosive, Black Doves is also surprisingly heartfelt, and you just can't help but root for its kooky cast. Even if they are all a bit nuts.

    Industry observers note that once you're on board the Harlan Coben train, it's hard to hop off. I Will Find You, led by Sam Worthington and Severance's Britt Lower, is certainly one of the better adaptations of a Coben novel. Ridiculous, for sure, but undeniably entertaining the second you suspend your disbelief.

    Five years after a man is wrongly imprisoned for the murder of his son, he receives information from his ex-wife's sister that his son might still be alive.

    It has been revealed that if you've read the book (or seen enough Coben highlights that you know what's coming), then maybe you won't be quite as surprised by the twists and turns in this one. That being said, it's breezy, easy-watching, and it's intensely bingeable if you're into that kind of thriller.

    Sources indicate that aside from the sense of humor, the thing we all love most about Guy Ritchie's films and others in that realm is the stylised action sequences. If that's what you'll be missing when MobLand is over, then give Gangs of London a watch.

    Based on the video game of the same name (but fortunately much better), the series revolves around the power struggles of rival gangs across London, all of which have different allegiances and international connections. When one young undercover police officer is tasked with infiltrating one of them to exploit a moment of weakness, things get ... very messy. Very fast.

    It's perhaps not as funny (read: not at all comedic) as some of the other entries on this list, but it's classically gritty, gory British crime drama at its finest, and a must-see for fans of the genre.
